Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

e-8572.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable
e-8572.problem:
Determine if the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/dfc9ee546f72ad68cf116b8f67d165ba9b6ff6e77dce88f145dda93f13091441.png)
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
e-8572.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=3.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-3I\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

e-8573.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
e-8573.problem:
Consider the following matrices:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/7126688b8500e60258d29ab4b1b323ac956ad41b530c5723bcc71d60b11e73a0.png)
Given that $D=P^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$
e-8573.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/f3460b47901f79529216c1440403e2115ff9047cb997070893b241cd938728de.png) we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1= -{2}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/95d1bcb284138711bcf5afddb3f09c702e664fbdc7b256b0eaf81044f87403cf.png)

By setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/898d72a1a0cc123d1ff7ecb4c8d02f6951739a9498e36ff14ee44cb322952fb6.png)

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-2}{1} = -2.$

e-8574.problem:
Given the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/8921e351c90855b6bf113a057eaa7e3ab97fbba8f22254463d894e7c4f89a4ed.png) 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D=P^{-1}AP.$
e-8574.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$$
\lambda_1=3, \quad\quad\lambda_2=-2.
$$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{8}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, $x_1$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_2=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/ff2073ee3866cfd3b40084ed4e676cc57554d9cd02b9d6e26cb7808f127fc56c.png)
Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/55c840d71fa907a9b372801123fdc7f19be810f2f489a2b167b0860c84d1c2cc.png)

- For $\lambda_2=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix corresponds to a homogeneous system of linear equations. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac{8}{5}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/3d52ed0fc48e2e20d268b6a49b099f8e3165f25707fa36aaf93c0e8b0a2c3b16.png)
Setting  $x_2=5,$ we get the eigenvector  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/ebb90bd7e57a148040b69a9fd6fd7d4f1b253e63734617e4e57b5177d7f9cda9.png)

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/4e04b534ec76c446059ca5119822b7aa299e0ea24c0e842de64a976954a733f8.png)

Question 1
?

Consider the matrix A=[68−4−6]. You're given that λ1=2 and λ2=−2 are the eigenvalues of A, and v1=[2−1], v2=[−11] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[2−200] and P=[21−1−1]
b
D=[200−2] and P=[2−1−11]
c
D=[02−20] and P=[2−11−11]
d
D=[02−20] and P=[2−1−11]
e
D=[−2002] and P=[21−11]
Submit

decision.explanation: Place the eigenvectors in the columns of P and their corresponding eigenvalues on the diagonal of D. This gives option b. Since det(P)=1 and AP=PD, P is invertible and PDP^{-1}=A.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the matrix A=[68−4−6]. You're given that λ1=2 and λ2=−2 are the eigenvalues of A, and v1=[2−1], v2=[−11] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[2−200] and P=[21−1−1]
b
D=[200−2] and P=[2−1−11]
c
D=[02−20] and P=[2−11−11]
d
D=[02−20] and P=[2−1−11]
e
D=[−2002] and P=[21−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=2 and λ2=−2, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[200−2].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=2, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−2.

Therefore, we get

P=[2−1−11].

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $H$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ b & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ b & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.

EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=4 and λ2=−2, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[400−2].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=4, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−2.

Therefore, we get

P=[5−371].

Finally, we obtain

H=[5−371][400−2][5−371]−1.

In conclusion, we get a=−2, b=7, and c=1.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $H$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ b & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ b & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=-2,$ $b=7,$ and $c=1.$

Question 3
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=3 and λ2=15 are eigenvalues, and v1=[12],v2=[−11] are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of a,b,c given that A=[1b2c][a0015][1b2c]−1?

a
a=15, b=−1, and c=−2
b
a=1, b=−3, and c=3
c
a=−1, b=3, and c=−3
d
a=3, b=1, and c=−1
e
a=3, b=−1, and c=1
Submit

decision.explanation: The first column (1,2) corresponds to eigenvalue 3, so a=3. Using the given second eigenvector (-1,1) gives b=-1 and c=1, hence option e. Option d is also valid because its second column is the negative of that eigenvector; scaling an eigenvector by -1 preserves the diagonalization.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=15$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ 2 & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ 2 & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=15,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=15.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=3,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=1.$

Question 3
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=3 and λ2=15 are eigenvalues, and v1=[12],v2=[−11] are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of a,b,c given that A=[1b2c][a0015][1b2c]−1?

a
a=15, b=−1, and c=−2
b
a=1, b=−3, and c=3
c
a=−1, b=3, and c=−3
d
a=3, b=1, and c=−1
e
a=3, b=−1, and c=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=3 and λ2=15, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[30015].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=3, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=15.

Therefore, we get

P=[1−121].

Finally, we obtain

A=[1−121][30015][1−121]−1.

In conclusion, we get a=3, b=−1, and c=1.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=15$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ 2 & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ 2 & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=15,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=15.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=3,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=1.$

before.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Question 4
?

Consider the matrix A=[5−2−14]. You're given that λ1=3 and λ2=6 are the eigenvalues of A, and v1=[11], v2=[2−1] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[3006] and P=[121−1]
b
D=[6003] and P=[211−1]
c
D=[−600−3] and P=[111−2]
d
D=[300−6] and P=[1211]
e
D=[−300−6] and P=[1211]
Submit

decision.explanation: Use the eigenvectors as columns of P and their corresponding eigenvalues as diagonal entries of D. Option a gives AP=PD and det(P)=-3, so P is invertible and PDP^{-1}=A.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the matrix A=[5−2−14]. You're given that λ1=3 and λ2=6 are the eigenvalues of A, and v1=[11], v2=[2−1] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[3006] and P=[121−1]
b
D=[6003] and P=[211−1]
c
D=[−600−3] and P=[111−2]
d
D=[300−6] and P=[1211]
e
D=[−300−6] and P=[1211]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=3 and λ2=6, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[3006].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=3, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=6.

Therefore, we get

P=[121−1].

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a: P has the given eigenvectors as columns, and D has their corresponding eigenvalues 3 and 6 on its diagonal. Since AP=PD and det(P)=-3, PDP^{-1}=A. The incorrect submission shown selected option d.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ c & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ c & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=-2,$ $b=3,$ and $c=-2.$

Question 5
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=−2 and λ2=−1 are eigenvalues, and v1=[1−2],v2=[3−4] are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of a,b,c given that A=[1bc−4][a00−1][1bc−4]−1?

a
a=2, b=−2, and c=3
b
a=1, b=−2, and c=3
c
a=2, b=3, and c=−2
d
a=−2, b=−2, and c=3
e
a=−2, b=3, and c=−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=−2 and λ2=−1, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[−200−1].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=−2, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−1.

Therefore, we get

P=[13−2−4].

Finally, we obtain

A=[13−2−4][−200−1][13−2−4]−1.

In conclusion, we get a=−2, b=3, and c=−2.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ c & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ c & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=-2,$ $b=3,$ and $c=-2.$

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is (1-λ)(5-λ)+3=λ²-6λ+8=(λ-2)(λ-4). The two distinct real eigenvalues imply A is diagonalizable, with D=diag(2,4), as in option a.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-(1)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +5+3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 7

Determine if the matrix A=[7−124−7] is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix D.

a
A is not diagonalizable
b
D=[7001]
c
D=[100−1]
d
D=[100−7]
e
D=[−700−7]
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is (7-λ)(-7-λ)+48=λ²-1, giving distinct eigenvalues 1 and -1. Therefore A is diagonalizable with D=diag(1,-1), which is option c.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -12 \\ 4 & -7\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -12 \\ 4 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )-4\cdot (-12) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 5 \\ -10 & -9\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 5 \\ -10 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-9-\lambda )-(5)(-10) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Determine if the matrix A=[65−10−9] is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[−1002]
b
D=[400−4]
c
A is not diagonalizable
d
D=[100−4]
e
D=[200−4]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix A by solving det(A−λI)=0:

|6−λ5−10−9−λ|=0(6−λ)(−9−λ)−(5)(−10)=0λ2+3λ−4=0(λ−1)(λ+4)=0

So, the eigenvalues are λ1=1 and λ2=−4. Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix A is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix D, as follows:

D=[100−4]

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable
content.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 5 \\ -10 & -9\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 5 \\ -10 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-9-\lambda )-(5)(-10) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & -4 \\ 24 & -10\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & -4 \\ 24 & -10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(-10-\lambda )-24\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix A by solving det(A−λI)=0:

|10−λ−424−10−λ|=0(10−λ)(−10−λ)−24⋅(−4)=0λ2−4=0(λ+2)(λ−2)=0

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable
content.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & -4 \\ 24 & -10\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & -4 \\ 24 & -10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(-10-\lambda )-24\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

after.problem:
Determine if the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-4I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & 5 \\ b & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of  $\frac{a}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

Question 11
?

Consider the following matrices: A=[−715−37],D=[−2002],P=[a5b3] Given that D=P−1AP, find the value of ab.

a
−12
b
13
c
−2
d
3
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the diagonal matrix D=[−2002], we deduce that the eigenvalues of A are λ1=−2 and λ2=2.

So, the first column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=−2.

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ1=−2. Computing A−(−2)I, we get

A−(−2)I=[−715−37]−(−2)[1001]=[−515−39].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−5150−390]R2:=R2+(−35)R1∼[−5150000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=3x2. Hence, the general solution is

[3x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector

v2=[ab]=[31].

Finally, ab=31=3.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
content.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & 5 \\ b & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of  $\frac{a}{b}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ -12 & 5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & a \\ -2 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ -12 & 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 \\ -12 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 0 \\ -12 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

before.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}10 & -12 \\ 8 & -10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & ∗ \\ -1 & ∗\end{aligned}]

decision.explanation: The second column must be an eigenvector for eigenvalue 2. Solving (A−2I)v=0 gives 8x−12y=0, satisfied by (3,2). Together with the first column (−1,−1), this gives det(P)=1, so P is invertible. Any nonzero multiple of (3,2) also works; option e is a valid choice.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}10 & -12 \\ 8 & -10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & ∗ \\ -1 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the second column of the matrix $P.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -12 \\ 8 & -10\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 8 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 & 0 \\ 8 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

So, the second column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=2.

A−2I=[10−128−10]−2[1001]=[8−128−12].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[8−1208−120]R2:=R2−R1∼[8−120000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=32x2. Hence, the general solution is

[32x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=2, we get the eigenvector

v2=[32].

Finally, P=[−13−12].

before.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 \\ ∗ & 1\end{aligned}]

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 \\ ∗ & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$   find the first column of the matrix $P.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$  

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 6 & -10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & a \\ 2 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 6 & -10\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 \\ 6 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 \\ 6 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$

Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 6 & -10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & a \\ 2 & b\end{aligned}]

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 6 & -10\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 \\ 6 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 \\ 6 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$

decision.explanation: For option a, B(1,2)=(1,2) and B(1,1)=−2(1,1), so BP=PD. Also det(P)=−1, hence P is invertible and PDP^{-1}=B.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$

Question 17
?

Given the matrix A=[2−103], find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[2003] and P=[1−10−1]
b
D=[2003] and P=[1101]
c
A is not diagonalizable
d
D=[2003] and P=[1−101]
e
D=[2003] and P=[2−2−11]
Submit

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues are 2 and 3. Corresponding eigenvectors are (1,0) and (−1,1), since A(1,0)=2(1,0) and A(−1,1)=3(−1,1). Option d uses these as columns of P, with det(P)=1, so AP=PD implies D=P^{-1}AP.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. On the other hand, from the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.html:
Question 17
?

Given the matrix A=[2−103], find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[2003] and P=[1−10−1]
b
D=[2003] and P=[1101]
c
A is not diagonalizable
d
D=[2003] and P=[1−101]
e
D=[2003] and P=[2−2−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix A is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:

λ1=2 and λ2=3

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=2, we have A−2I=[2−103]−2[1001]=[0−101]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[0−10010]R2=R2+R1∼[0−10000]. The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 2nd one). Thus, x1 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x2=0. Hence, the general solution is [x10],x1∈R. Setting x1=1, we get the eigenvector v1=[10].

  • For λ2=3. Then A−3I=[2−103]−3[1001]=[−1−100]. So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. On the other hand, from the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is [−x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector v2=[−11].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P as follows: D=[2003],P=[1−101].

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. On the other hand, from the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 18
?

Given the matrix A=[−3−20−2], find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[200−2] and P=[1−20−1]
b
D=[3002] and P=[−1−201]
c
D=[2003] and P=[1201]
d
D=[−300−2] and P=[1−201]
e
D=[−200−3] and P=[−1−301]
Submit

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues are −3 and −2. Their respective eigenvectors (1,0) and (−2,1) form the columns of P in option d. Since det(P)=1 and AP=PD, D=P^{-1}AP.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the matrix A=[−3−20−2], find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[200−2] and P=[1−20−1]
b
D=[3002] and P=[−1−201]
c
D=[2003] and P=[1201]
d
D=[−300−2] and P=[1−201]
e
D=[−200−3] and P=[−1−301]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix A is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:

λ1=−3 and λ2=−2

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=−3, we have A−(−3)I=[−3−20−2]+3[1001]=[0−201]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[0−20010]R2:=R2+12R1∼[0−20000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 2nd one). Thus, x1 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x2=0. Hence, the general solution is [x10],x1∈R. Setting x1=1, we get the eigenvector v1=[10].

  • For λ2=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−3−20−2]+2[1001]=[−1−200]. So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−2x2. Hence, the general solution is [−2x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector v2=[−21].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P as follows: D=[−300−2],P=[1−201]

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 19
?

Find matrices P and D such that PDP−1=B, where D is a diagonal matrix and B=[12−1−2].

a
D=[0001] and P=[−23−1−1]
b
D=[100−1] and P=[21−1−1]
c
D=[200−1] and P=[21−11]
d
D=[000−1] and P=[21−1−1]
e
D=[000−1] and P=[20−1−1]
Submit

decision.explanation: For option d, B(2,−1)=(0,0) and B(1,−1)=−(1,−1), so BP=PD. Since det(P)=−1, P is invertible and PDP^{-1}=B.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ -1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-2\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Find matrices P and D such that PDP−1=B, where D is a diagonal matrix and B=[12−1−2].

a
D=[0001] and P=[−23−1−1]
b
D=[100−1] and P=[21−1−1]
c
D=[200−1] and P=[21−11]
d
D=[000−1] and P=[21−1−1]
e
D=[000−1] and P=[20−1−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix B using its characteristic equation det(B−λI)=0:

|1−λ2−1−2−λ|=0(1−λ)(−2−λ)−2⋅(−1)=0λ2+λ=0λ(λ+1)=0

So, the eigenvalues of B are λ1=0 and λ2=−1.

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of B.

  • For λ1=0, we have B−0I=[12−1−2]−0[1001]=[12−1−2]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[120−1−20]R2:=R2+R1∼[120000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−2x2. Hence, the general solution is [−2x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=−1, we get the eigenvector v1=[2−1].

  • For λ2=−1, we have B−(−1)I=[12−1−2]−(−1)[1001]=[22−1−1]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[220−1−10]R2=R2+(12)R1∼[220000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is [−x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=−1, we get the eigenvector v2=[1−1].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P as follows: D=[000−1],P=[21−1−1]

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ -1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-2\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

a
A is not diagonalizable
b
D=[−2005] and P=[−1142]
c
D=[−2005] and P=[1−124]
d
D=[−2002] and P=[1−504]
e
D=[−2002] and P=[−5140]
Submit

decision.explanation: For option e, A(−5,4)=(10,−8)=−2(−5,4) and A(1,0)=2(1,0). Thus AP=PD. Since det(P)=−4, P is invertible and D=P^{-1}AP.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=4,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{4}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=4,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
